label: Anger and Resentment
framing: Scripture does not forbid all anger, but it puts a clock on it and a guard around it. The aim is not a person who never burns but one who rules his own spirit, which it ranks higher than taking a city.
cultural: In the honor-shame world of the Bible, an insult demanded retaliation and a hot temper was often admired as strength. Into that, the wisdom writers called the slow fuse a higher courage, and Jesus traced murder back to the anger in the heart, scandalizing a culture that measured sin only by the deed.
historical: The desert fathers of the fourth century named anger one of the deadly thoughts and watched how it actually moves in a person. Thomas Aquinas, in the thirteenth century, distinguished righteous anger at real wrong from the disordered anger that serves the self, a distinction the church has kept ever since.
application: Put a delay between the heat and the word, since the rash sentence costs more than any enemy. Ask what is under the anger, usually a fear, a wound, or a thwarted want. Do not bank it overnight, where it hardens into contempt. And when it is righteous, aim it at the injustice rather than at the person nearest you.

verses.text: “Why are you angry,” said the LORD to Cain, “and why has your countenance fallen? If you do what is right, will you not be accepted? But if you refuse to do what is right, sin is crouching at your door; it desires you, but you must master it.”
verses.where: Cain is angry that God accepted his brother's offering and not his own. God speaks to him before anything has happened, asks why he is angry, and warns that sin is crouching at his door. The first anger in the Bible is met with a question and a warning, not a curse.

verses.text: Jesus looked around at them with anger and sorrow at their hardness of heart. Then He said to the man, “Stretch out your hand.” So he stretched it out, and it was restored.
verses.where: In a synagogue on the Sabbath, religious leaders watch to see whether Jesus will heal a man's withered hand so they can accuse him. Jesus is angry, and grieved, at the hardness of their hearts, and he heals the man. Anger here is aimed at harm done to someone else, and it ends in mercy.

verses.text: My beloved brothers, understand this: Everyone should be quick to listen, slow to speak, and slow to anger, for man’s anger does not bring about the righteousness that God desires.
verses.where: James writes to believers living under pressure. He does not say never be angry. He says be slow to it, and quick to listen, because human anger does not produce the righteousness God wants, even when the cause feels righteous.

verses.text: Be angry, yet do not sin; on your bed, search your heart and be still. Selah
verses.where: A psalm of David prayed in distress. The anger is not denied. It is taken to bed and searched in silence before God, instead of being spent on someone.

verses.text: A gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.
verses.where: A saying about how quarrels grow or die. A gentle answer is not weakness; in Proverbs it is the stronger move, because it turns away wrath that a harsh word would feed.

verses.text: He who is slow to anger is better than a warrior, and he who controls his temper is greater than one who captures a city.
verses.where: In a world that prized warriors and conquerors, this saying ranks the person who controls his temper above them. Ruling yourself is the harder victory.

verses.text: A man’s insight gives him patience, and his virtue is to overlook an offense.
verses.where: A saying for the small daily offenses. Insight brings patience, and overlooking an offense is called a person's virtue, not a loss.

verses.text: But the LORD replied, “Have you any right to be angry?”
verses.where: Jonah is furious that God has spared Nineveh, the enemy city he was sent to warn. God answers his anger with a question, and the book ends with God's own question about compassion. Anger often hides a quarrel with mercy.

verses.text: Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but leave room for God’s wrath. For it is written: “Vengeance is Mine; I will repay, says the Lord.”
verses.where: Paul writes to Christians who would face real wrongs. He does not say the wrongs do not matter. He says leave the repaying to God, who judges justly, and quotes Deuteronomy to make the point.

verses.text: Get rid of all bitterness, rage and anger, outcry and slander, along with every form of malice. Be kind and tenderhearted to one another, forgiving each other just as in Christ God forgave you.
verses.where: Paul describes the new life in a church: truthful speech, honest work, kind words. Bitterness, rage and slander are to be put away, and kindness and forgiveness put on, with God's forgiveness in Christ as the pattern.

misread.taken: This verse gets read two opposite ways. Some take it to mean that all anger is sin. Others treat “Be angry” as permission for whatever comes out, or turn the sunset into a rule that every quarrel must be settled before bedtime.
misread.says: Paul is quoting Psalm 4:4, which uses the same words. Anger itself is assumed, not commanded or forbidden: be angry, and do not sin in it. The sunset line reflects a common ancient view that a dispute should be settled before the day ends. The point is not a curfew but a warning about time. Anger left to sit overnight, night after night, hardens into bitterness and gives the devil a foothold, a place to stand in your life and in your relationships.
misread.text: “Be angry, yet do not sin.” Do not let the sun set upon your anger, and do not give the devil a foothold.

misread.taken: Jesus driving the traders out of the temple is sometimes used to defend any outburst as “righteous anger.”
misread.says: Jesus' action was about God's house turned into a marketplace, and his disciples connected it with zeal for that house (John 2:17). It was not a reaction to a personal insult. Anger that is about God's honor and other people's harm looks very different from anger about being slighted, and most daily anger is the second kind.
misread.text: So He made a whip out of cords and drove all from the temple courts, both sheep and cattle. He poured out the coins of the money changers and overturned their tables.

whole: Anger is quick and it feels like strength. It can fill a home with tension long after the shouting is over. People who struggle with it often know two things at once: that something really was wrong, and that what they did with it made things worse. Some have stopped saying anything at all, and the anger has turned into a quiet bitterness that leaks out sideways.

The Bible does not treat anger as always sin. God is angry at injustice, and Jesus was angry at hearts that would rather keep a rule than see a man healed. But Scripture is wary of human anger, because it so easily serves the self while calling itself justice. From Cain onward, anger is described as something crouching at the door, a power that wants to rule the one who feels it. Underneath it there is often hurt, fear, or a sense of being owed something, and there is often a quarrel with mercy, like Jonah's.

The wisdom of Scripture is to take anger seriously without obeying it. Be slow to it and quick to listen. Bring it to God before you bring it to the person, and search your heart in the quiet. Name the real wrong honestly, and leave the repaying to God. Answer gently, overlook what can be overlooked, and do not let it sit night after night until it becomes who you are. Where the anger is about real harm to someone, it may need to become action for justice. Where it is about you, it usually needs to become forgiveness.

differ.share: Christians agree that God's anger at sin is holy and just, that human anger is dangerous and easily sinful, and that bitterness and revenge have no place in the Christian life.

views.name: Wary of all human anger
views.body: Some Christians, drawing on James 1:20 and a long tradition of counsel on the passions, are wary of nearly all human anger and teach that it should be quieted rather than used.

views.name: Room for anger at injustice
views.body: Others point to the prophets and to Jesus in Mark 3, and hold that anger at injustice can be right and can move people to act, as long as it is aimed at the wrong and not at revenge.

differ.after: Both agree that most everyday anger is not of the righteous kind, and that the test is what it is aimed at and what it produces.

deep.sit: The last time you were angry, what were you afraid of losing, and what did you believe you were owed?

prayer.lead: A one-line prayer from Psalm 141 for the moment before you speak.
prayer.text: Set a guard, O LORD, over my mouth; keep watch at the door of my lips.
